newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN content with boost in Croat-rebel Serb links. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UN content with boost in Croat-rebel Serb links. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]

text.p: The United Nations said on Thursday it was satisfied with positive developments in relations between Croatia and its breakaway Serb minority in their last U.N.-controlled enclave.
Philip Arnold, spokesman for the U.N. Temporary Administration of Eastern Slavonia region (UNTAES) said five offices had been opened in the region for issuing Croatian papers to local residents.
Eastern Slavonia, monitored by some 5,000 U.N. peacekeepers, is due to revert to Croatian rule some time next year.
"Some 5,000 people came to the offices in the first three weeks to apply for various papers - birth certificates, passports or identity cards," Arnold told a news conference in Zagreb.

Most of the applicants in the first week were ethnic Croats, he said. Up to 10,000 Croats have remained in Eastern Slavonia after it was captured by the Serbs at the outset of the 1991 war following Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia.
"But after that there have been increasingly more Serbs," he said, adding the U.N. planned to arrange a mobile office in a van that would visit Serb villages.
Arnold praised a general amnesty law passed by the Croatian parliament last week pardoning all who took part in the Serb rebellion against Croatia's independence, save war criminals.

"We are pleased with the new amnesty law. It appears to meet our requests for a broad and general amnesty... This should give a sense of confidence to the people in the region," he said. But he added the response from local Serbs had so far been subdued.

The UNTAES will next week begin a "weapons buy-back programme" under which it will buy weapons from local Serbs, store them in U.N. depots and turn them in to Croatian authorites at the end of its mandate.

The mandate officially expires on January 15 (corrects date of mandate expiring from December). Croatia has agreed to extend it for another three months, while local Serbs demand another year. The matter will ultimately be resolved by the U.N. Security Council, Arnold said.
In another positive development, joint Croat-Serb customs control units will start operating in the next few weeks.
"They are being trained together as we speak," Arnold said.
